channel.title: Sell to the Past
channel.description: I'm a merchant with a time machine. Each episode I take one thing we buy without thinking and try to sell it to people in the past. How many days of work would they pay? And what does it cost us today? 8 minutes, real numbers with sources.
channel.itunes:author: Sell to the Past

item.title: I tried to sell a litre of water to a man who sells water in 1854. Then I said one word
item.description:
I took a one-litre bottle of tap water, worth a fifth of a cent in the US, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a water carrier in cholera-era London, to a water carrier in Paris before the Revolution, and to a sailor in the middle of the ocean in 1812. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what water really costs.
Chapters: 0:00 The bottle and the rules 0:35 London, 1854: William 3:00 Paris, 1785: Jacques 5:30 The ocean, 1812: Tom 7:30 Back to today
Sources: - US EPA WaterSense, national average water rates: https://www.epa.gov/watersense/data-and-information-used-watersense - US federal minimum wage: https://www.usa.gov/minimum-wage - All historical sources are listed in research/research.md of the episode (Wellcome Collection, John Snow archive, Paris Musées, USS Constitution Museum). Images: Wikimedia Commons, public domain / CC (credit on screen).

item.title: I tried to sell a supermarket loaf of bread to people in 1795. Here's what they paid
item.description: A standard sliced loaf costs about $2.30 in the US, or 19 minutes of work at the federal minimum wage. In this first episode I take it into a time machine and try to sell it three times: to a farm labourer in England in the hungry summer of 1795, where a loaf cost five hours in the field; to a builder in Rome in 301 AD, where the wheat in a loaf cost two hours but white bread was status; and to a clerk in Paris under siege in 1870, where 300 grams a day were rationed and no money bought more. The best buyer wasn't the richest. All numbers with sources in the description.
